t.1.166.1: The Gandharva said: In this world there was once a king called Kalmāṣapāda, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, O Pārtha, unequalled on earth in splendor.
t.1.166.2: Once that king went out from the city to the forest for the hunt; that crusher of enemies roamed about, piercing deer and boars.
t.1.166.4: The unconquered one saw, in the fray, a sage coming toward him face to face, the illustrious Śakti by name, the delight of Vasiṣṭha's lineage, the eldest of the hundred sons of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha.
t.1.166.3: But that king, afflicted by thirst and afflicted by hunger, having come onto a path wide enough for only one, came upon the great-souled Vāsiṣṭha, the best of seers, on the way.
t.1.166.5: "Get out of our path!" thus the king spoke. The seer, in turn, addressed him, soothing him with gentle words.
t.1.166.6: But the seer, standing firm on that path of dharma, did not step aside; nor did the king give way before the sage, out of pride and out of anger.
t.1.166.7: But that best of kings, out of folly, then struck with his whip the seer, the sage who would not yield the path, as a rākṣasa would.
t.1.166.10: "Attached to human flesh, you shall roam this earth; go, O lowest of kings!" Thus was he addressed by Śakti, whose power lay in his might.
t.1.166.12: As the two of them were quarreling thus, O Pārtha, the mighty seer Viśvāmitra, of fierce austerities, approached them.
t.1.166.11: Then enmity arose between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha over the matter of a sacrificial patron, and at that time Viśvāmitra sought him out.
t.1.166.13: Then afterward that best of kings recognized the seer as the son of the seer Vasiṣṭha, one who was like Vasiṣṭha himself in splendor.
t.1.166.14: Then Viśvāmitra too, O Bhārata, making himself invisible, approached the two of them, wishing to accomplish what was dear to himself.
t.1.166.15: But that best of kings, thus cursed by Śakti, went to Śakti for refuge, honoring him and seeking to win his favor.
t.1.166.16: Having understood the intention of that king, O delight of the Kurus, Viśvāmitra then directed a Rākṣasa against the king.
t.1.166.17: Then, because of the curse of that brahmin seer and at the command of Viśvāmitra, a Rākṣasa named Kiṃkara entered into the king.
t.1.166.18: But knowing that he had been seized by the Rākṣasa, the sage Viśvāmitra then departed from that region, O tamer of foes.
t.1.166.19: Then that wise king, guarding himself by his own effort, though he was mightily oppressed by the Rākṣasa that had entered within him,
t.1.166.20: A certain twice-born man saw that king as he was setting out once more, and, being hungry, he then begged him for a meal with meat.
t.1.166.21: Then the royal sage Mitrasaha, soothing that brahmin, said to him: "Wait right here for a moment, O brahmin."
t.1.166.22: "When I have returned, I will give you food as you desire." Having said this, the king went forth, and the best of the twice-born remained there.
t.1.166.24: Then, rising at midnight, the king had the cook brought to him in haste and, remembering what he had promised the brāhmaṇa, spoke to him.
t.1.166.23: But then the brahmin's words slipped from the king's mind, and the lord of men, entering the inner apartments, lay down to rest.
t.1.166.25: Go! In that place yonder a brāhmaṇa is waiting for me, wanting food; you must provide him with food together with meat.
t.1.166.26: Thus addressed, the cook, unable to find meat anywhere, then reported this, filled with distress, to that king.
t.1.166.27: But the king, possessed by the Rākṣasa and free of all distress, said to the cook again and again, "Feed him with human flesh!"
t.1.166.28: Saying "So be it," the cook then went quickly to the place of the executioners and, free of fear, carried off human flesh.
t.1.166.29: Having duly prepared it and quickly set it out together with food, he gave it to that hungry brāhmaṇa ascetic.
t.1.166.30: Having seen that food with his perfected sight, that best of the twice-born, his eyes agitated with anger, said, "This is not fit to be eaten."
t.1.166.31: Since that lord of men gives me food that is not fit to be eaten, that very fool shall therefore have a craving for it.
t.1.166.32: Addicted to human flesh, just as Śakti had declared before, he will roam this earth, a source of terror to all beings.
t.1.166.34: Then that best of kings, his senses overpowered by the Rākṣasa, saw Śakti and, as if almost at once, spoke to him, O Bhārata.
t.1.166.33: When it had been pronounced a second time, that curse upon the king became powerful, and then, possessed by the might of the Rākṣasa, he lost his senses.
t.1.166.35: Since this unfitting curse has been laid upon me by you, I shall therefore begin to devour men, starting with you.
t.1.166.36: Having spoken thus, he then at once deprived Śaktin of his life-breaths and devoured him, as a tiger devours a coveted beast.
t.1.166.37: Seeing Śaktin slain, Viśvāmitra then once again directed that Rākṣasa against the other sons of Vasiṣṭha.
t.1.166.39: Having heard that those sons of his had been caused to be slain by Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha bore that grief as a great mountain bears the earth.
t.1.166.38: Enraged, he devoured those hundred younger sons of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, as a lion devours small animals.
t.1.166.40: That best of sages set his mind on his own destruction, but the best of the wise never once considered the extermination of the Kuśikas.
t.1.166.41: The blessed seer cast himself down from a peak of Meru, and his head fell upon the rock as though upon a heap of cotton.
t.1.166.42: And when he did not die from that fall, O Pāṇḍava, the blessed one then kindled a fire in the great forest and entered it.
t.1.166.43: Then the oblation-eating fire, though well kindled, did not burn him; though blazing, O slayer of foes, the fire became cool.
t.1.166.44: Overcome with grief, the great sage went to the ocean, tied a heavy stone to his neck, and threw himself into its waters.
t.1.166.45: That great sage, set down upon dry land by the force of the ocean's waves, then went, dejected, back once again toward his hermitage.
t.1.166.8: Then that best of sages, the son of Vasiṣṭha, struck by the blows of the whip and overwhelmed with rage, cursed that best of kings.
t.1.166.9: Since you strike an ascetic like a Rākṣasa, O vilest of kings, from this day forth you shall become an eater of men.
